newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO official says Hebron deal possible on Monday.
newsitem.headline: PLO official says Hebron deal possible on Monday.

text.p: Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met Palestinian negotiators and a PLO official said he expected a deal over Hebron would be reached later on Monday.
"We expect a deal tonight. Negotiations are continuing," said Jamil Tarifi while entering talks on Hebron between Israeli and PLO officials. He did not elaborate.
Earlier, chief Palestinian negotiator Mahmoud Abbas, also known as Abu Mazen, said the sides were edging closer to a deal. "There is progress," Mazen said after talks with Netanyahu.
Netanyahu, who convened his senior ministers on Monday to discuss Hebron, was scheduled to meet with U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross at 1730 GMT, Netanyahu's office said.
Ross was due to brief Netanyahu on talks he held in Cairo with Egyptian officials on Monday.
Asked about the possibility of an agreement on Israeli troop redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron being reached, Ross told reporters before leaving Egypt:
"It is more feasible now. It's a possibility but not a final thing. The negotiators are working hard. The issues are being discussed but nothing final has been drafted."
PLO officials said Abbas would convey a letter to Arafat from Netanyahu, but they did not say what it contained.
Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai told reporters after talks with Netanyahu on Monday evening that Israel was "more optimistic" now.
"We have all been optimistic for a very long time already. We'll be a little more optimistic," Mordechai said when asked if an agreement was pending.

In Hebron, an Israeli truck took camp beds and equipment from the military governor's office but officials declined to say whether final preparations for a long-delayed troop redeployment were under way.
Only six military vehicles were left at the office, the nerve centre of Israel's military occupation of Hebron since 1967, reporters said.

Palestinian officials had said there was agreement on some major disputed points, but other issues were left to be resolved in a meeting yet to be arranged between Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
Arafat himself said a meeting might take place on Monday night.
Ross, who arrived in the Middle East on Saturday saying he hoped to re-energise talks, had played down hopes of a breakthrough.

Israel and the PLO have accused each other of foot-dragging in more than three months of talks on Hebron, 80 percent of which was due to have been handed over to Arafat's Palestinian Authority months ago.

Netanyahu, who came to power in June vowing to take a tough line on Israeli security, has demanded protection for 400 Jewish militants in the heart of the city of 100,000 Arabs, a longtime flashpoint of violence between Arabs and Jews.

PLO officials said the Israelis had dropped their insistence on having the right of hot pursuit of Palestinian suspects into PLO-held areas, accepting instead existing language in the Hebron handover agreement signed in 1995.

One PLO official said agreement had also been reached to reopen Martyrs Street in the heart of town within four months. It has been closed to Palestinians. It was also agreed to reopen the long-closed vegetable market so long as it was a retail rather than a wholesale market.
